articles.title: Cooking with Anna Haugh: ‘A langoustine is easy to make outstanding, but a carrot takes skill’
articles.summary: The MasterChef judge on artichokes, ambition and Irish food. It’s an amazing moment when Anna Haugh lets me peel and chop a butternut squash, right there in the kitchen next to her, while she makes a beetroot pickle.
body: Elite cooking while talking like a Bren gun is a skill she’s honed, first in cookery demos “talking to a plastic bag and a stray dog, and you’d be lucky if someone came over to shelter from the rain”; then on Saturday Kitchen – a trial by fire: “Everything is easy after that. I could do any cookery programme now. I even tried to persuade them to do the MasterChef final live.”

Haugh grew up in Tallaght, a working-class suburb of Dublin, the youngest of four, her dad an engineer, her mother an incredible home cook who made everything from scratch, including things nobody ever makes, like cereal. “She taught us how to cook as a life skill,” says Haugh. “It was about nutrition and economy. Dad was the foodie.”

articles.title: Pickled Celery Gibson
articles.summary: A Gibson usually substitutes a cocktail onion for the olive. This version features easy homemade pickled celery and has the same clean, briny qualities as the classic.
body: From Victorian celery vases to midcentury relish trays, celery has been part of hosting parties in the United States for many generations. At gatherings hosted by my grandma Dorothy in western New York in the ’90s, I remember big stalks of celery resting in pitchers of salt water in the middle of every table, acting as both a palate-cleansing snack and a centerpiece. Similarly, this recipe for pickled celery can function as a garnish (consider skewering it onto a cocktail pick with a cornichon and a cherry tomato for a Bloody Mary), part of a canapé, or just as a snack on its own.

In a small saucepan over low heat, combine ½ cup [120 ml] distilled vinegar, 1 tsp. kosher salt, 1 tsp. sugar, 2 garlic cloves, 1 tsp. black peppercorns, 1 clove, and ¼ tsp. coriander seeds with ½ cup [120 ml] water. Cook for about 5 minutes, until the sugar and salt are dissolved. Place 4 celery stalks (about 200 g), cut into 1½" [4 cm] lengths, in a heatproof bowl, and pour the hot brine over it. Allow the mixture to cool to room temperature, then transfer it to an airtight container. Refrigerate at least overnight before using, and store, refrigerated, for up to 1 week.

articles.title: 30 Sparkling, Fringed, and Pleated Holiday Wedding Guest Dresses for Every Festive Fête
articles.summary: Do you have a holiday wedding coming up? From gold lamé to swishy fringe, these festive gowns cover every dress code, from brands like Kallmeyer, J. Crew, and Tory Burch.
body: Weddings during the holiday season come with a built-in sense of joy. The venue is likely already decked out in garlands and candlelight, everyone is in a celebratory mood, and if the date falls on New Year’s Eve, there’s a midnight countdown baked right into the reception. Your outfit should match that energy. While standard winter guest attire often leans moody, a December through February fête (don’t forget about Valentine’s Day nuptials!) leaves plenty of room to play—think rich textures, high-shine finishes, and statement silhouettes.

Of course, a few standard wedding-guest rules still hold true. Steer clear of anything that reads as bridal—that includes winter white, no matter how tempting a cream silk slip might be. Skip the costume-like details, too: A ruby-red J.Crew mini feels spirited, while a tinsel-trimmed ensemble in the same shade can quickly veer kitschy. Beyond that, pay attention to the dress code, as that will dictate your hemline; minis and midis are fair game for less formal invitations, especially when paired with tights and a great heel. And don’t forget about a chic evening coat that’ll tie your outfit together.

articles.title: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love Wrapping Gifts
articles.summary: Since going through a major breakup last year, I’ve tackled all kinds of things that I didn’t previously know I could do. Was it possible that I could also become the kind of person who looked forward to—or at least didn’t totally dread—my very least favorite Christmas chore, wrapping presents?
body: I am one of the messiest people I know, and I come by that reputation honestly. Legend has it that when my parents first met at a party at my mom’s apartment, my dad walked up to her to say that she should probably call the police; he’d passed her bedroom while in search of the bathroom and seen the window wrenched open, with belongings strewn all over the floor. He suggested that she report a robbery—but no, she was forced to admit; that was just how she lived.

I’ve inherited her struggles with neatness and attention to detail. While other mother-daughter duos brought in perfectly stenciled posters and Balthazar-quality brownies to class presentations and bake sales, our attempts were somewhat more haphazard, typically following screaming fights in the aisles of the Staples on 81st and Broadway about what qualified as “nice” graph paper.

articles.title: The Rise, Fall, and Future of Makeup Artist-Led Brands
articles.summary: Rather than chasing $1 billion valuations or flooding shelves with limited-edition drops, modern makeup artist-led brands such as Violette and Katie Jane Hughes are focused on tight, high-performing SKUs to outlast trend cycles.
body: When news broke in October that Isamaya Ffrench had severed ties with her namesake beauty brand, fans of the avant-garde makeup artist were saddened but not surprised. For months, there had been growing customer frustration about unfulfilled orders and unresponsive support. Buyers reported severe shipping delays, missing or damaged items, and unanswered refund requests across the brand’s Instagram and review sites like Trustpilot. By July, its social media accounts had stopped creating new posts, while inventory markdowns on its website were as high as 70%.

Ffrench responded to a customer complaint on Instagram in October by apologizing, adding that she was no longer associated with the brand. Shortly after, she thanked her followers on her personal Instagram during what she called “an incredibly difficult and emotional time”. The Isamaya Beauty brand did not respond to a request for comment.

articles.title: Herby Cottage Cheese Scones
articles.summary: These garden-­inspired scones are a hit year round, but extra special in the spring and early summer when fragrant herbs grow rampant
body: This is the kind of recipe that necessitates a mild-­tasting flour such as Sonora wheat, ensuring nothing takes away from the delicate herbs. In addition to Sonora or other soft wheat flour, I use refined all-­purpose flour and fine yellow cornmeal. You’ll find yourself mincing herbs to add to the mix. Make sure to use a sharp chef’s knife that won’t bruise the herby bits; this helps them retain their flavor and aroma. Roasting the scallions softens and caramelizes them a bit. I also add lemon zest and cracked black pepper. Both play a supporting role, never overpowering the herbs. To finish, garnish with a few flakes of crunchy salt, such as Maldon.

Smeared with butter, cream cheese, or even more cottage cheese, these scones are a dreamy addition to a weekend breakfast or afternoon tea. They also pair perfectly with smoked salmon or egg salad. For an elegant appetizer, they can be baked into smaller versions of themselves (see the variation that follows).
